title: How a case becomes a precedent
bodyMd:
A judicial decision cannot guide later cases until someone describes what it decided. That description may seem a clerical task: extract the rule and apply it again. Yet a decision usually contains more facts than any later dispute will repeat. Choosing which facts matter is already an interpretive act. A summary that seems broad enough to cover a new dispute may omit a qualification that mattered greatly to the earlier court. A summary narrow enough to repeat every circumstance may leave the decision with no application beyond itself. The difficulty is therefore not solved by choosing either maximal generality or maximal detail. A later interpreter must explain why a particular description preserves the reasons that made the earlier outcome intelligible. The rule is not simply found lying apart from the facts; it is articulated through an account of their significance.

Imagine an earlier court refusing to enforce a penalty in a contract between a large supplier and an inexperienced customer who had no realistic alternative source. A later judge might describe the decision as protecting inexperienced parties, as responding to unequal bargaining power, or as limiting penalties when meaningful choice is absent. Each description fits some features of the earlier case, but each points toward a different range of future applications. A sophisticated small firm may lack alternatives; an inexperienced customer may have many. The level of generality changes which similarities count.

This does not make precedent empty or infinitely flexible. The earlier court gave reasons, and those reasons constrain plausible descriptions. If its opinion emphasized the lack of alternatives while expressly declining to rely on experience, a later account centered solely on inexperience would be difficult to defend. Other decisions can also reveal whether a proposed description fits a wider pattern or is a convenient exception invented for the present dispute.

The discipline of precedent therefore lies neither in mechanical repetition nor in unrestricted analogy. It requires making the bridge between cases explicit: identifying the earlier reasons, explaining which features bear on them, and showing why a difference is or is not relevant. Disagreement can remain after this work, but it becomes disagreement about an articulated inference. To say that precedent involves judgment is not to say that any judgment is equally faithful to it.
